title: DoFlow: Forecasting with Causal Interventions
one_liner: A generative model predicts not just what will happen, but what will happen if you intervene to change the system.
lead: Most forecasts answer: what comes next? But real systems need causal forecasts: what comes next if we stop the factory? When will the patient recover if we try treatment A versus treatment B? DoFlow learns a causal map of the system and predicts under any scenario—normal, intervened, or counterfactual.

problem.h2: Why normal forecasts fail under intervention
paras: A standard time-series model learns: given the last few measurements, predict the next measurement. It learns from the past: if temperature keeps rising, keep rising. But the moment you intervene—you flip a switch, you give a drug—the past patterns break. The model has no idea what happens next because the intervention is something new it has never seen.

What a beginner tries: train a bigger model on more data, or add more features. But this does not work because the model learned only correlation, not causation. Correlation means: when A goes up, B goes up. Causation means: A makes B go up. A normal forecaster confuses them. If you turn off the thing that makes A go up, the correlation disappears, but a non-causal model still predicts it will happen—dead wrong.

callout.html: Learn the causal structure of the system (which variables cause which) and predict through that structure, so interventions get the right answer.

panels.title: 1. The system has hidden causes
panels.caption: Temperature, pressure, valve state: variables linked by cause-and-effect.

panels.title: 2. Standard model learns correlations only
panels.caption: All variables move together, but model does not know why.

panels.title: 3. Causal structure maps causes
panels.caption: Causal DAG: each arrow is a real causal link between variables.

panels.title: 4. Intervene: block a cause
panels.caption: Turn the valve off: pressure and temperature drop, not from correlation, but causal truth.

panels.title: 5. Prediction flows through the causal graph
panels.caption: Generative model samples futures respecting causal links, even under new interventions.

steps.text: Infer or assume a directed acyclic graph (DAG) showing which variables cause which.
Build a reversible neural network that maps random noise to realistic time-series trajectories, respecting causal order.
When you see the first few time steps, compress them into a starting point in the model's latent space.
Clamp certain variables (the intervened ones) to their new values, then decode the rest.
Sample from the model to generate multiple plausible futures under the intervention or counterfactual scenario.

paras: Standard generative models predict one random future at a time. DoFlow goes further: it makes those predictions conditional on a causal graph and on interventions. It changes how the model's latent space (the compressed representation of the system) respects causality.

hidden.h2: Causal sufficiency: the true path through the system
hidden.name: Causal graph and counterfactual recovery
paras: The hidden quantity is the causal structure itself—the directed acyclic graph (DAG) where each arrow means one variable truly causes another. This graph is invisible in the data; you see only correlations. The paper assumes you either know the DAG or infer it from domain knowledge or statistical tests.

Once the graph is fixed, DoFlow uses it to predict what happens under intervention. It learns a counterfactual recovery function (a learned mathematical operation) that takes an observation and a hypothetical intervention and outputs what the system would have done under that intervention instead.

heat.caption: Darker: directly in the causal chain of prediction. Bright: noise or measurement artifact.

reads.html: The causal graph is a map of the system: which levers control which outcomes. If you know the map, you can predict what happens when you pull a lever, even if it is a lever you have never pulled before.
The paper learns a flow-based distribution over time series that factorizes according to the causal DAG: the generative process respects the causal order, so interventions are naturally supported.

mechanism.h2: Why changing the latent representation to follow causality fixes the problem
paras: Standard generative models (like diffusion or VAEs) learn to map noise to data, but they do not respect causality. They learn the marginal distribution: what patterns happen in the real data. But causality is about conditional distributions: what happens given an intervention.

DoFlow uses a normalizing flow (a reversible neural network) that factorizes according to the causal DAG. This means the generative process—the path from noise to samples—follows the causal order: first it generates the root causes, then the things they cause, then the effects of those effects. Because the generative process respects causality, when you intervene (clamp a variable to a new value), the rest of the model automatically propagates the consequences correctly.

This works because the flow model learns the true conditional probabilities implicit in the graph. When you say the valve is now OFF (an intervention), the model does not just pattern-match to "valve off" from the training data; instead, it recomputes pressure and temperature via the causal edges that actually depend on the valve. It is not predicting from correlation; it is computing from the causal graph.

stages.s: Generate root causes (valve state, pump speed)
Clamp intervened variables to new values

math.words: The generative process samples from a prior distribution and transforms it through a series of invertible neural-network layers that are ordered by the causal graph: each layer generates variables conditioned on their causal parents, then passes control to the next layer.
math.equation: x = f(z; theta), where f is invertible and factorizes as f(z) = [f_root(z_root), f_child_1(z_c1; x_parents), f_child_2(z_c2; x_parents), ...], with log p(x) = log p(z) - log |det J_f|
symbols: the time-series trajectory we want to generate
the part of the flow that generates root causes (variables with no parents in the DAG)
the part that generates the ith child variable conditioned on its parents
the log probability (how likely the trajectory is under the model)
the Jacobian (the matrix of how f's outputs change with inputs)
the change in volume as we transform from noise space to data space

worked.title: Tiny worked example: two variables with causal link
lines: Causal graph: Valve → Pressure (valve causes pressure).
Sample z_valve = 0.5 (noise for valve), z_pressure = -0.3 (noise for pressure).
f_child computes: pressure_value = neural_net_2(-0.3, valve=0.8) = 2.4 (high pressure because valve is open).
If we intervene: set valve to 0.1 (closed), then f_child recomputes: pressure = neural_net_2(-0.3, valve=0.1) = 0.6 (low pressure).
Same noise, different valve intervention, different pressure outcome—causality is preserved.

math.note: The factorization respects the DAG order, so each variable depends only on its causal parents, and interventions automatically propagate downstream.

items.html: If the assumed DAG is incorrect, predictions under intervention will be wrong. For example, if you think pressure causes valve position, but it is the reverse, the model will predict the wrong future when you intervene on the valve.

If two variables are both caused by a third variable you did not measure (a confounder), the causal graph will be misspecified. This breaks counterfactual recovery, because interventions will not account for the hidden cause.

If you never see interventions in the training data, the model cannot learn how the system behaves under intervention. It will generalize poorly to new interventions, even with the correct causal graph.

If the causal graph is known (from domain experts or from randomized experiments), and the flow model is trained on realistic data, it will forecast accurately under new interventions and counterfactuals.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple 3-variable system: a heater (on/off), a room temperature (rises when heater on), and a thermostat reading (tracks temperature, but lags by 1 step). Generate 1000 time steps of data with random on/off decisions. Train a standard LSTM forecaster and DoFlow on the same data. Then: (1) Forecast the next 10 steps in a normal scenario (heater on randomly). (2) Intervene: force the heater off and forecast 10 steps. (3) Ask a counterfactual: if the heater had been on 5 steps ago instead of off, what would the temperature be now? Standard model will fail on steps 2 and 3. DoFlow should succeed because it learned the causal graph (heater causes temperature, temperature causes thermostat).
demo.metric_eq: Accuracy on counterfactual trajectories = (number of time steps where prediction is within 10% of ground truth) / (total time steps in counterfactual query)
demo.closing: The demo proves that causality is learnable and that a causal model generalizes to interventions the training data never saw.
